hints: Look closely at the C=C double bond on the left and check whether the two carbon chains lie on the same side or opposite sides.
The alcohol part of the ester is the -O-CH(CH3)2 group, so work out the structure of alcohol X as HO-CH(CH3)2 and count carbons on the C-OH carbon.
Combine the same-side or opposite-side result for cis or trans with the primary, secondary or tertiary classification to pick the matching row.
walkthrough:
**Identify the geometrical isomerism at the C=C**

Look at the left-hand alkene part: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2-$. The two larger carbon groups, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-$ on the left and $-\text{CH}_2\text{C=O}$ on the right, are drawn on the same side of the double bond.

Same side means cis (Z) isomer, opposite sides would mean trans (E).

**Split the ester to find alcohol X**

Ester formation is:
$$\text{carboxylic acid} + \text{alcohol} \rightarrow \text{ester} + \text{water}$$
The acyl side is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{C(=O)}-$, the alkoxy side is $-\text{OCH(CH}_3)_2$.

So alcohol X must have been $\text{HO-CH(CH}_3)_2$, which is propan-2-ol.

**Classify alcohol X**

Classification depends on the carbon bearing the -OH group. In $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{CH-OH}$ the C-OH is joined to two other carbon atoms.

Joined to 2 carbons means secondary alcohol. Cis plus secondary matches one row exactly.

options.A: Correct. The two alkyl groups are on the same side of the C=C, so it is the cis isomer. Alcohol X is (CH3)2CH-OH, propan-2-ol, where the OH carbon is attached to two carbons, so it is secondary.
options.B: Incorrect. Cis is right, but tertiary is wrong. A tertiary alcohol needs the C-OH attached to three carbons, such as (CH3)3C-OH. Here the group is -OCH(CH3)2, from a C-OH with only two carbons.
options.C: Incorrect. Secondary is right, but trans is wrong. Trans requires the two chains to be on opposite sides of the double bond. In the diagram they are bent to the same side, giving cis.
options.D: Incorrect on both parts. The alkene is cis, not trans, and the alcohol is secondary, not tertiary. This choice confuses the bent cis shape with trans and miscounts the carbons on the alcohol carbon.
